problem: Unemployment benefits were seen as complex and a possible disincentive to take short-term work.
title: Finland tests an unconditional basic income with 2,000 unemployed people
context: Finland wanted to test whether an unconditional payment could improve employment and reduce benefit complexity.
decision_made: Pay 2,000 unemployed people aged 25 to 58 a monthly EUR 560 with no conditions, for two years.
action_taken: Ran a randomised experiment in 2017 and 2018 with a control group on ordinary unemployment benefit.
observed_outcome: Employment effects were small: recipients averaged about 49.6 days in work against 49.3 for the control group. Recipients reported greater life satisfaction and less mental strain.
observation_period: Two years, final report in May 2020
lessons: A basic income may improve reported wellbeing without much effect on employment over two years.
limitations: A new activation model in 2018 complicates reading the employment effects. The wellbeing survey had no baseline, so changes cannot be attributed to the payment with certainty.

sources.publisher: Ministry of Social Affairs and Health

claims.claim_text: Finland paid 2,000 unemployed people EUR 560 a month without conditions in a 2017-2018 experiment.
Employment effects were small while recipients reported better wellbeing.
